question_text: A 56-year-old woman comes to the office due to generalized muscle weakness and muscle cramps. Medical history is significant for Sjögren syndrome, but she takes no medications. Physical examination shows mild muscle weakness. Laboratory results are as follows: Serum potassium decreased Serum bicarbonate decreased Serum anion gap normal Urinary ammonium excretion decreased Which of the following best explains the laboratory findings in this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Increased production of systemic endogenous acids

options.label: E
options.text: Resistance of distal tubule to aldosterone effect

explanation.text:
The kidneys can excrete a limited amount of acid as free H⁺; therefore, most H is excreted in the form of ammonium (NH₄⁺). This patient with hypokalemia, nonanion gap metabolic acidosis (ie, decreased serum bicarbonate [HCO₃⁻]), and decreased urinary ammonium excretion most likely has type 1 renal tubular acidosis (RTA), a potential complication of autoimmune disease (eg, Sjögren's syndrome) involving impaired acid excretion (eg, H⁺-ATPase dysfunction) by alpha-intercalated cells of the distal tubule. Type 1 RTA creates a nonanion gap metabolic acidosis, as do all types of RTA, due to retention of H⁺⁺ and a net loss of HCO₃⁻ . Impaired distal tubular acid secretion also leads to increased K⁺ excretion and consequent hypokalemia. Urine pH is >5.5 due to markedly impaired ability to acidify the urine, and muscle weakness may develop due to hypokalemia. In addition, metabolic acidosis can leach calcium from bones, causing osteomalacia and increasing urinary calcium excretion. Compared to other types of RTA, type 1 carries particular susceptibility loss of HCO₃⁻ . develop due to hypokalemia. to calcium-phosphate nephrolithiasis, likely because the less acidic urine pH encourages calcium stone formation.

(Choice B) Impaired (not increased) proximal tubule HCO- reabsorption is the cause of type 2 RTA. As with type

1, nonanion gap metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia develop, but urine pH is more acidic (ie, <5.5) because intact distal H excretion compensates somewhat for the impaired proximal HCO₃⁻- reabsorption (ie, urine ammonium excretion is normal).

(Choice C) Increased production of systemic endogenous acids (eg, lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis) creates

an anion gap metabolic acidosis. High urinary ammonium excretion is expected (assuming the kidneys are functioning normally) as the kidneys try to excrete excess acid.

(Choice D) Alveolar hypoventilation causes respiratory acidosis. In response, the kidneys increase ammonium

excretion to increase serum HCO₃⁻ and create a compensatory metabolic alkalosis.

explanation.educational_objective: Type 1 renal tubular acidosis results from impaired distal tubular excretion of H⁺ (in the form of ammonium [NH₄⁺]). Patients typically have nonanion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, and markedly impaired ability to acidify the urine with urine pH >5.5.
